name: muParser
baseline: TinyExpr (also muParserX, Lepton, MTParser, MathExpr; it loses to ExprTk, METL and FParser in the same suite)
workload: Evaluate pre-parsed expressions (parse once, evaluate many times) with variables a, b, c, x, y, z, w in the third-party math-parser-benchmark-project; 74 expressions from bench_expr.txt, each evaluated 5,000,000 times, ranked per expression and points summed.
claimed_speedup: README example for '(a^2/sin(2*pi/b))-a/2': muparser 2.2.4 47.358 ns, TinyExpr 121.184 ns, Lepton 297.673 ns, muparserx 498.809 ns (muparser about 2.6x faster than TinyExpr, derived from page data). Example summary scores: muparser 2.2.4 517 points (score 37), TinyExpr 354 (31), MTParser 381 (34), MathExpr 360 (29), Lepton 134 (8), muparserx 86 (5), versus FParser 4.5 584 (43) and ExprTk 901 (100). Committed 2018 log for bench_expr.txt: muparser 523 points, TinyExpr 360, MTParser 383, MathExpr 364, Lepton 136, muparserx 85.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC Version 1913 (Visual Studio 2017), Release, 32-bit build (flags are not printed in the result logs); the repo's math-parser-benchmark-project.pro builds with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -fopenmp and -O3 for C sources, with HAVE_STDINT_H and MUP_USE_OPENMP defined
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W 0 @ 3.10GHz, 8 cores / 16 logical, L3 20480 KB, 3092 MHz
tradeoffs: Bytecode interpreter over a parsed expression (parse once, evaluate many), not a JIT or compiler; mutable variable bindings, user callbacks and optional OpenMP over expression arrays. The muparser repo has no benchmark of its own; the README only says 'fast math parser library'.
caveats: Weak and mixed result: muparser is mid-pack (6th of 13 entries by points on bench_expr.txt) and loses to ExprTk, METL, FParser and atmsp in the same suite, so 'faster' holds only against TinyExpr, MTParser, MathExpr, Lepton and its own heavier sibling muParserX. The suite is maintained by ExprTk's author, a competitor, and bundles muparser 2.2.4 (the README says the archive 'may contain outdated versions'); current muparser is newer, so the numbers may not apply. The 'omp' variant is slower than plain muparser in every log read. Windows 32-bit MSVC only for the logged results; the README-visible summary is labelled an example. The project's own site (beltoforion.de) is blocked from this session, so any first-party performance page was not read. Licence note: the benchmark README lists muParser as MIT; the repo LICENSE read today is BSD-2-Clause.

name: NumKong
baseline: GCC 12 auto-vectorized loops (f32 and _Float16); also NumPy 2.4 + OpenBLAS, PyTorch 2.10 + MKL and JAX 0.9
workload: Single-threaded 2048-d dot products and 2048x2048 matrix multiplication across f64, f32, bf16, f16, e5m2 and i8 on Intel Sapphire Rapids, plus inner product, cosine, Euclidean and Jensen-Shannon kernels on f16 versus GCC 12 auto-vectorized code.
claimed_speedup: Dot product (2048-d): f32 7.1 gso/s versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 1.5 (about 4.7x, derived from page data), PyTorch+MKL 0.6, JAX 0.4; f64 5.8 versus 2.0; f16 11.5 versus 0.2 (NumPy), 0.5 (PyTorch); i8 14.8 versus 1.1 (NumPy, overflowing). Matmul 2048x2048: i8 1279 gso/s versus PyTorch+MKL 50.0; e5m2 398 versus 0.4; but f64 8.6 versus 65.5 (NumPy+OpenBLAS) and 68.2 (PyTorch+MKL), f32 37.7 versus 140 and 145, bf16 458 versus 851 (PyTorch). GCC 12 table: f16 inner product 5,990 K/s versus GCC f16 192 K/s (31x) and GCC f32 3,810 K/s (about 1.6x, derived); Jensen-Shannon f16 2,140 K/s versus GCC f16 18 K/s (118x). Binary size: 5 MB versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 30 MB, JAX 357 MB, PyTorch+MKL 705 MB.
compiler_and_flags: Only 'GCC 12' stated for the auto-vectorization table, no flags; NumPy 2.4, PyTorch 2.10, JAX 0.9 for the library table. The repo builds with -march=x86-64 plus per-function target pragmas and -fno-tree-vectorize for its own serial fallbacks (CONTRIBUTING.md); bench/README.md gives the cmake commands for nk_bench.
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids (microarchitecture only, no exact CPU model), single-threaded
tradeoffs: 2,000+ hand-written SIMD kernels across x86, Arm, RISC-V, LoongArch, Power and WebAssembly with runtime dispatch; mixed-precision widening accumulators (f16 to f32, f32 to f64, i8 to i32) and compensated f64 Dot2 summation change numerical results versus plain same-type accumulation; caller-owned threads and buffers; no general BLAS API.
caveats: First-party README tables with partial methodology, so tier C: the CPU is named by microarchitecture only, no flags or run counts for the library tables, and the 'gso/s' unit counts integer and float work together. Baselines are Python frameworks (NumPy, PyTorch, JAX) for the headline tables, not C++ std::vector loops; Python call overhead is part of the single 2048-d dot product row. The matrix multiplication table is mixed: NumKong is slower than OpenBLAS and MKL for f64 (8.6 versus 65.5 and 68.2 gso/s), f32 (37.7 versus 140 and 145) and bf16 (458 versus 851). The GCC 12 comparison uses plain auto-vectorized loops on _Float16, which is a weak baseline; against GCC f32 the f16 kernels win by only about 1.6x on inner product. NumKong's repo-level benchmark (bench/README.md) mostly compares its own SIMD backends against serial code, not other libraries. The sibling NumWars repo (broader cross-library comparisons by the same author) was not opened.

name: pixz
workload: Compress and decompress a 3 GB CSV file (about 17 million tweets) through the R package pRDS's command-line wrappers at default levels (xz = 6), on a 4-core, 8-thread i7 Mac.
claimed_speedup: pRDS README benchmark table: pixz write 443 s, read 63 s, size 805 MB versus xz write 469 s, read 64 s, size 795 MB (pixz about 1.06x faster to compress and about 1.02x faster to decompress, derived from page data; output 1.3% larger, derived). Other rows: 7z 580 s write, 83 s read, 741 MB; R native xz 2626 s write, 105 s read, 772 MB (pixz about 5.9x faster than R's built-in xz, derived from page data). The pixz README itself gives no numbers, only the claims that pixz parallelizes decompression and defaults to all cores while xz defaults to one.
hardware: i7 Mac, 4 cores / 8 threads (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Splits input into independent xz blocks (loses some compression ratio versus one large block, 805 MB versus 795 MB in the table above), adds a tarball index for fast listing and single-file extraction, output is a normal .xz stream with an added index; needs libarchive and liblzma; flags differ from xz (-z, -c, -f, -l, -q, -t mean different things).
caveats: Weak evidence: one loosely controlled run by a third party (the pRDS author says 'not in an entirely scientific manner', 'loosely controlled environment', and that four tools did not work as intended on the machine), no tool versions, no flags, no CPU model, no repeat runs. The 'xz' row is not stated to be single-threaded or multi-threaded (the 469 s figure is plausible for single-threaded xz -6 on 3 GB), and a 6% gain from 8 threads suggests pixz was not parallelizing well in that setup. Modern xz (5.2 and later) has its own -T threading, so the pixz README's 'xz defaults to one core' framing is now only a default difference. The pixz repo has no benchmark of its own and the README makes no speed numbers. Directional only; filed to record that no stronger public pixz-versus-xz measurement was reachable (pxz and pigz benchmark pages found by search were not pixz-specific, and the neurolabusc/pigz-bench README does not cover xz or pixz).
